chapters.title: Chapter 4: Cross-Sectional Momentum - Ranking and Rotation

lessons.title: Building a Relative Strength Ranking System

children.text: The last two lessons covered what cross-sectional momentum is and why it works academically. This lesson builds one, end to end: choosing a universe, choosing a ranking metric, applying the skip-month convention from Chapter 1, and turning a ranked list into an actual portfolio. The single biggest design choice in the whole process, whether to rank by raw return or by risk-adjusted return, changes which stocks the system actually picks more than almost any other decision.

body.text: A relative strength ranking system is five decisions, not one: the universe to rank, the metric to rank by, how to handle the most recent month, how often to rebalance, and how to size positions across the ranked list. Change any one of these and the resulting portfolio changes with it, sometimes dramatically.

children.text: A Nifty 50 universe is liquid and cheap to trade, but as Chapter 1 covered, heavily analyst-covered large caps tend to show a weaker momentum effect precisely because their information diffuses faster. A broader universe, the Nifty 500 or the Nifty Midcap 150, has historically shown a stronger raw momentum effect, at the cost of worse liquidity, wider bid-ask spreads, and higher market impact when entering or exiting a position, all real costs that eat into the larger headline return.

Ranking purely by trailing return rewards any stock with a big move, including one driven by a single volatile spike that is unlikely to repeat. A risk-adjusted momentum score fixes this by dividing trailing return by the stock's own volatility over the same window, rewarding a smooth, sustained climb over an erratic one with the same headline return. This is close to the actual approach used by the Nifty200 Momentum 30 Index, introduced in Chapter 1, which scores stocks using volatility-adjusted trailing returns rather than raw return alone.

body.caption: A risk-adjusted momentum score: trailing return over the formation window divided by that same stock's volatility over the same window, conceptually similar to a Sharpe ratio computed just for the formation period.

children.text: As covered in Chapter 1, the most recent month is typically excluded from the formation window, since stocks often show short-term reversal right after a sharp move, noise that would otherwise contaminate the ranking. A 6-month formation window in practice usually means months t-7 through t-1, not t-6 through t.

Rebalancing monthly keeps the portfolio's holdings closely aligned with the freshest ranking, but generates more turnover and more transaction costs. Rebalancing quarterly or semi-annually, closer to how published indices like the Nifty200 Momentum 30 operate, cuts costs and turnover at the price of holding a slightly staler ranking between reconstitution dates. There is no universally correct answer, it is a direct trade-off between signal freshness and cost, one this course returns to more formally when covering transaction costs and backtesting later on.
Step 5: Portfolio Construction, How Many and How Weighted

Equal-weighting the selected names, the same rupee amount in every stock in the top decile or top N, is simple and doesn't concentrate risk in whichever single name happens to score highest. Score-weighting, allocating more capital to higher-ranked names, tilts the portfolio more heavily toward the strongest momentum signals but concentrates risk in fewer names and is more sensitive to any single position's reversal. Most practical systems, including many published momentum indices, use some form of score-based weighting with a cap on any single position's maximum size, a middle ground between the two extremes.
Worked Example: Raw Return vs Risk-Adjusted Ranking
Take eight hypothetical stocks from a broader universe, each with a 6-month trailing return and its own volatility over the same window.

body.caption: Eight hypothetical stocks: raw return vs risk-adjusted momentum score (illustrative)

body.text: The top 3 stocks by raw return are S, V, and P, the three biggest headline movers. The top 3 by risk-adjusted score are Q, R, and T, none of which overlap with the raw-return top 3 at all. S and V had the largest returns but also enormous volatility to go with them, while Q, R, and T climbed more modestly but far more smoothly. This single design choice, raw return versus risk-adjusted score, produces two completely different portfolios from the exact same underlying data.

body.caption: A simple risk-adjusted ranking pipeline
body.code:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.DataFrame({
    "return": [0.45, 0.38, 0.30, 0.60, 0.20, 0.15, 0.50, 0.25],
    "volatility": [0.35, 0.22, 0.18, 0.55, 0.15, 0.40, 0.48, 0.20],
}, index=["P", "Q", "R", "S", "T", "U", "V", "W"])

data["momentum_score"] = data["return"] / data["volatility"]
data["rank"] = data["momentum_score"].rank(ascending=False)

top_n = 3
selected = data[data["rank"] <= top_n]
weights = pd.Series(1 / top_n, index=selected.index)  # equal-weighted

print(data.sort_values("momentum_score", ascending=False))
print("\nSelected portfolio (equal-weighted):")
print(weights)

body.title: Calculate a momentum score
body.prompt: A stock returns 42% over its 6-month formation window, with a volatility of 30% over the same period. What is its risk-adjusted momentum score, to two decimal places?
body.explanation: 42 / 30 = 1.40. Dividing trailing return by volatility over the same window produces the risk-adjusted momentum score used to rank stocks in Step 2 of this lesson.

body.title: Why did Stock S rank poorly on a risk-adjusted basis?
body.question: In this lesson's worked example, Stock S had the highest raw 6-month return, 60%, but ranked only 6th out of 8 on the risk-adjusted score. Why?
options: Because the momentum score formula does not use return at all
Because Stock S's volatility, 55%, was so high that it dragged the return-to-volatility ratio down despite the large headline return
Because Stock S's data was excluded due to the skip-month convention
Because raw return and risk-adjusted score always produce the same ranking
body.explanation: A momentum score divides return by volatility. Stock S's return was large, but its volatility was large enough, 55%, to pull the ratio down to 1.09, well below smoother performers like Q and R, which had lower returns but far lower volatility.

cards.definition: A momentum ranking metric that divides trailing return by volatility over the same window, rewarding smooth, sustained trends over erratic ones with the same raw return.
The defined set of stocks a ranking system selects from and ranks against each other, such as the Nifty 500 or Nifty Midcap 150.
How often a ranking system re-scores its universe and updates its holdings, trading off signal freshness against transaction costs.
A portfolio construction approach that allocates more capital to higher-ranked names rather than weighting every selected position equally.

points: A relative strength ranking system requires five real decisions: universe, ranking metric, skip-month handling, rebalance frequency, and position weighting.

Ranking by risk-adjusted momentum score, return divided by volatility, rather than raw return alone can select a completely different set of stocks, favoring smooth, sustained trends over erratic, volatile spikes.
This approach mirrors how published indices like the Nifty200 Momentum 30 are actually built, not just an academic simplification.
Rebalance frequency and universe choice both trade signal quality against real-world transaction costs, a theme this course returns to when covering backtesting and costs directly.
Equal-weighting is simpler and avoids concentration risk, while score-weighting tilts more capital toward the strongest signals at the cost of more concentration.
